newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany approves ground-breaking Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: Germany approves ground-breaking Bosnia force.

text.p: Germany on Friday gave its soldiers the final go-ahead to join a new Bosnia peacekeeping force, the first time German combat forces will take full part in a ground mission alongside Western allies.

With a large part of the opposition also in favour, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government secured an overwhelming 499-93 majority in parliament for the motion to send some 3,000 soldiers to join the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR).

The 18-month deployment is the first time dedicated combat troops from united Germany will serve on the ground in another country in the kind of mission which is almost commonplace for the United States, France and Britain.
"The end of our special role is a relief, not only for our soldiers," Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told parliament.
"Germany is fully living up to its obligations to NATO and the U.N. -- good news for all those who believe in a common European purpose and stronger international cooperation."

The decision is also the culmination of Kohl's step-by-step campaign to get public acceptance for the shedding of post-war West Germany's inhibitions, born of the horrors of Nazi militarism, about sending any forces whatsoever abroad.
Bonn had about 4,000 troops in the multinational IFOR mission whose mandate expires on December 20.

But it limited their tasks to logistical jobs such as bridge building and running a field hospital because of fears they might revive memories of the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia and the brutal repression of Serb partisans in World War Two.

In addition, they were stationed in Croatia rather than Bosnia to avoid any possible confrontations with Serbs. The only potential combat mission was an airborne one by German fighter pilots maintaining a no-fly zone over Bosnia.
"We have now seen that, contrary to some people's fears, our soldiers' presence is welcomed by all sections of the population," Kinkel said.
The new German contingent will be the fourth-largest after those of the United States, Britain and France, and work closely with French troops in the French-administered sector of Bosnia.

For the first time it will include 2,000 infantry and armoured vehicle-borne reconnaissance forces ready and equipped to face combat situations. A German two-star general will serve as Chief of Staff under the American mission commander.
It is a situation Germany's leaders could not have imagined even in 1991, when they paid $5.5 billion rather than send troops to join a multinational force to drive Iraq from Kuwait.

Since World War Two, the only German combat troops to have served on the ground abroad were the communist East German forces sent to Czechoslovakia to help the Soviet Army put down the liberal "Prague Spring" in 1968.
Even the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) have now largely abandoned long-cherished pacifist tendencies to support the idea of sending troops on multinational missions.
But the U.N. Security Council still got the government out of a tight spot by approving SFOR's mandate late on Thursday.
The SPD had threatened to boycott Friday's debate if the U.N. resolution had not been passed, arguing that parliament had a right to know exactly what it was saying 'yes' to.
"We are not taking just any old decision," SPD foreign affairs spokesman Guenter Verheugen told parliament.
"It may mean that we must take responsibility for our young people losing their health or their lives. Can any one of us then come back and say 'I didn't know what the mandate was'?"
